title: How, and why
hookLine: years one to three told the story, and this year asks how Muslims live it and think it through
last: YOU ARE IN THE STORY NOW.

lines: A STRANGER IN WHITE, KNEE TO KNEE.
WHAT IS ISLAM? WHAT IS FAITH?
HE CAME TO TEACH BY ASKING.
cards: Medina, a gathering already under way. A stranger walks in, his clothes startling white, his hair very black, no dust of travel on him, and nobody there knows who he is.
He sits down in front of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, close, knee to knee, and starts asking questions. What is Islam? What is faith?
What is it to do good? The Prophet answers each one. Then the man goes.
Later the Prophet tells his companions who it was: the angel Jibril, come to teach them their religion. He taught it with questions.

teach.b: That report is recorded in Sahih Muslim, and it gives this year its shape. The first three years told the story: the Qur'an's words, the Prophet's life, the people and the centuries after.
Year four turns from what happened to how. How do Muslims pray, fast, give, travel to Mecca? And why: why these words, why this order, why do scholars sometimes disagree?
First, the plan: the pillars, one by one, starting tomorrow with the testimony.

Then the ways of thinking that grew around them: how reports of the Prophet are judged, law and its schools, belief, the inner life, and the shape of a life from birth to death. Second, questions are welcome.
The Qur'an tells its first hearers, in Pickthall's translation: "Ask the followers of the Remembrance if ye know not." Asking is part of how the religion gets handed on.

Even the Prophet is told to keep asking for more: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Third, how sits next to why. You can learn the movements of the prayer in an afternoon; the why can take a lifetime.

teach.h: THE DOING AND THE WHY, TOGETHER.
teach.b: The Jibril report keeps the two side by side: islam, the doing, and faith, the inner yes, asked about one after the other. Fourth, this year describes; it doesn't decide.
Where Sunni and Shia Muslims practice differently, or the schools of law part ways, you'll hear who says what, plainly, and nobody ranked.
Someone who has prayed for decades and someone who has never seen a prayer mat can both bring a question.

how: Muslims learn how to practice from parents, imams and teachers, and some bring their questions to a scholar or a study circle; the report of Jibril's visit can be taught as a summary of the whole religion, told through questions.

games.q: a stranger sits knee to knee with the Prophet and asks him question after question, about things everyone around already practices. what's going on?
o: a test of the Prophet's patience.
a visitor who never got an answer.
games.why: the Prophet later said it was Jibril, come to teach them their religion: the questions were the lesson.

practice: Let questions come about how Muslims live, or why they do what they do: a small one, like why shoes come off at the door of a mosque, or a big one, like what it means to say God is one.
Don't answer them; just catch three, and hold on to them for the year ahead. If you pray, you can ask for understanding in your own words.

wordCard.voice: How. The question this year keeps asking: how Muslims live their faith, and, right beside it, why. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: bring your questions. Every one of them is welcome here. Tomorrow, two sentences.
